english.html: lity, who was a woman, who is frightened and terrified at a small thing <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>, and moreover lets herself easily be persuaded — and in her, persuasions have no less force than threats or force <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>. Added to which also, she daily made complaint of it against her said stepfather and mother <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>.

notes.citation: The Gloss and the Doctors on Decretals X 4.1 (De sponsalibus et matrimoniis), c. Cum locum (X 4.1.14)
notes.original: La gloſe & les Docteurs. au c. cum locũ de ſponſa.
notes.gloss: Consent has no place where fear or coercion intervenes; the commentators there discuss the fear that can move a steadfast woman.

notes.citation: Digest, a title printed de in ius. (perhaps De in ius vocando, D. 2.4), l. 1, § Usque adeo — not identified; Code 9.13 (De raptu virginum, seu viduarum, nec non sanctimonialium), the sole law (C. 9.13.1, Justinian), at the words Volentibus
notes.original: l j. P. vſque adeo. D. de in ius. l. vnique. en ces paroles, Volẽtibus. C. de rap. virgi.
notes.gloss: Justinian punishes the ravisher even where the women were willing, the will of a woman being easily bent — Coras's point that persuasion works upon a woman as force does. The print's vnique is vnica, the sole law.

notes.citation: Digest 29.2 (De adquirenda vel omittenda hereditate), l. Qui in aliena, the last paragraph (cf. D. 29.2.6, Ulpian; paragraph unverified), and the Interpreters there
notes.original: l. qui in aliena. P. fin. D. de aquir. hære. & les Interpretes.
notes.gloss: The bearing of the fragment on complaint as proof of compulsion could not be verified.

notes.original: l. ad beſtias D. de pœn.
notes.gloss: Those condemned to the beasts are not to be released to please the crowd; but if they are of such strength or skill that they may worthily be exhibited to the Roman people, the governor is to consult the emperor — the malefactor's excellence in his kind earning him a reprieve, which is Coras's ironic point.

english.html: Fifthly, the accused having been, for other deeds, made prisoner by authority of the Seneschal of Toulouse, and at the instance of Jean d'Escornebœuf, called the Cadet — the said Pierre Guerre always underhand supplying every favour and aid — this deed too was advanced against him; whereof the same de Rols complained incessantly against the said Pierre Guerre and his wife, who wished to constrain her to accuse the same accused, being resolved to have him put to death, or at the least to have him put in the Galleys. And when he had come out of prison, by virtue of the interlocutory order upon contrary facts [appointement de contraires: an order admitting the parties to prove their contrary allegations] given by the said Seneschal, being back at Artigat, the said de Rols received him and made much of him as her husband; and as soon as he had arrived, gave him a white shirt, nay, washed his feet, and afterwards they lay together.

The ruse of this rogue is marvellous, and such that, if ever a malefactor could deserve some excuse for being excellent and sovereign in his kind of artifice and wickedness, this one would be worthy of it above all oth
